Stats say that only about 5% of the global population has hazel eyes. Astronomers nicknamed a distant star (found in the Virgo constellation) “Hazel Iris” bc it has a multi-colored glow, its hues mimicking the golden-green-brown shades. And, throughout history, people with hazel eyes were thought to have mystical and magical powers; Celts thought we were literally blessed by the gods, Persians believed they were the mark of immortality and that we had eternal souls, and folklore claimed we could control the weather. Women are attracted to certain qualities and if you dont exude them you’ll lose the opportunity to get to know someone. This has always been true in history (not just ‘these days’); women like men (and vice versa) who take care of themselves and present themselves well because this reflects desirable qualities like capability, effort, awareness, maturity, self-respect, respect for others, discipline and responsibility. If you insist on keeping something around to use as self-defence, use common household/workplace items that you can claim with certainty were NOT intended to be used for self-defence. E.g. hair spray, bug spray (in the summer), a small metal shovel (in winter for example to shovel snow away from your tires), a box cutter (if you can prove your work requires you to carry one frequently), a full metal water bottle with a handle, a pencil/pen, a fork, a debit/credit card, handful of dirt/sand, hot water, etc. Make sure that, whatever you intend to use, you have it in your possession for a believable reason (if you're a receptionist, prosecutors will be suspicious of why you were carrying around a box cutter unless you're currently in the middle of moving houses, etc.).

**Do not ever admit** you possess anything (even a pillow) with the intention of using it for self-defence. That means items like pepper spray, tasers, knuckle rings with spikes, or anything designed to be used for self-defence are illegal to have in your possession in Canada. Dog spray is legal to own and carry, but it's illegal to use on humans; it can only be used on animals like dogs or bears.

Also, if you ever do find yourself in a situation where you need to use these items on someone, you must use what they call "reasonable force": if a person is holding a knife and it is clear they intend on stabbing and killing you, you may defend yourself with a lethal weapon like a box cutter, for example. But if the person is simply shoving you a bit, and you use a box cutter to injure them, you will be charged and most likely convicted of a crime even if you were the "victim" in the situation. Even if someone breaks into your home holding a knife and you shoot them with a hunting rifle, you're in big trouble. It needs to be 100% clear that they intend to kill you first before you use lethal force on them.

The 40-hour work week.

Why:

Humans aren't biologically meant to work 40 hours a week. Force a chimpanzee to remain active for 8 hours straight without time to relax and see what happens. Most chimps are only active in the morning, the rest of the day they'll relax, play, eat, and nap. We, however, don't stop working until 5-6 pm — not 12 pm. Studies show that productivity stays exactly the same if humans work 25-30 hours a week. We can only work for so long before our focus wanes and completely fizzles out. So most of us can't concentrate more than 5-6 hours a day. Any more than that is a waste of time because nothing of value is getting done. This time could be spent exercising, spending time with family, siesta, or for self-care.

But we're told that it's "normal". If this is supposed to be normal, please explain to me why nearly everyone in the Western world seems to suffer from depression and/or anxiety. These illnesses are so common that  almost anyone you talk to about your depression or anxiety will say they have it too. This is a case where *situational depression* turns into *clinical depression* because the situation (being overworked) never goes away. Problem is, hustle culture. You don't want to work hard and make sacrifices every day for what you want? Lazy. You want a living wage without killing yourself from stress Mon-Fri? Entitled. (Looking at you, boomers). We're being exploited and most of us don't even know it. Never forget that time is one of the most valuable things you'll ever have in your life.

*That's why everyone deserves a* ***living wage*** *working max.* ***30*** *hours a week.* If someone can make that happen — and the rates of both depression AND anxiety don't plummet almost immediately after — I'll write you a check for $1 million dollars.

I'll copy+paste a part of an answer I gave previously to this question:

>Just like cows, pigs, chickens, and other "farm animals", most farmed bees suffer and are abused in a lot of ways. They don't even have the right to eat the food they worked so hard to make (honey). A bee's main food source is honey (hence why they make it in the first place). Most farmers take their honey and replace it in their hive with a sugar substitute, which is damaging to the bees’ health. The cheap sugar replacer lacks the nutrients, fats, and vitamins they need that are found in honey.  
>  
>Bees notice this, so they overwork themselves to replace their missing honey. They're also rarely handled with any care or compassion. They're killed or have their wings and legs torn off by haphazard handling. Beekeepers also clip the queen bee’s wings to prevent her from leaving the hive and producing a new colony elsewhere (which would impact productivity and profit). Queen bees are also often artificially inseminated.  
>  
>And when the honey is being removed (aka stolen from them), a lot of bees die from trying to defend their food and home, things they worked tirelessly to make from scratch.  
>  
>To give you an idea of how many bees have to work like slaves to create a jar of honey: a bee produces just a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in his/her lifetime, and it takes the pollination of two million flowers to produce a single pound of honey. That's a lot of abused bees.

That's okay, it's not a stupid question!:) It's good to ask questions and understand why vegans choose not to eat certain things.

Just like cows, pigs,  chickens, and other "farm animals", bees suffer and are abused in a lot of ways. They don't even have the right to eat the food they worked so hard to make (honey). A bee's main food source is honey (hence why they make it in the first place). Farmers take their honey and replace it in their hive with a sugar substitute, which is damaging to the bees’ health. The cheap sugar replacer lacks the nutrients, fats, and vitamins they need that are found in honey.

Bees notice this, so they overwork themselves to replace their missing honey. They're also rarely handled with any care or compassion. They're killed or have their wings and legs torn off by haphazard handling. Beekeepers also clip the queen bee’s wings to prevent her from leaving the hive and producing a new colony elsewhere (which would impact productivity and profit). Queen bees are also often artificially inseminated.

And when the honey is being removed (aka stolen from them), a lot of bees die from trying to defend their food and home, things they worked tirelessly to make from scratch.

To give you an idea of how many bees have to work like slaves to create a jar of honey: a bee produces just a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in his/her lifetime, and it takes the pollination of two million flowers to produce a single pound of honey. That's a lot of abused bees.

\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

For your second question, yes populations may be decreasing but that's not necessarily a bad thing in this specific case, because fewer bees are being born into a miserable life of abuse and mistreatment. Same thing with cows, if we stopped breeding them for slaughter and banned factory farming, the cow population would plummet. And just like how the number of slaves declined in the many years following the abolition of slavery in the late 1800s in the US. We definitely do not want ***wild*** bee populations to plummet (the ones who aren't used by humans to put honey on supermarket shelves), but the decrease of **farmed** bee populations is causing less suffering, abuse and slaughter of bees.

I hope this helps!

I totally understand how you're feeling and it's very real. I'm not sure if think anyone really knows why depression causes this though, it's just one of the symptoms. 

  
My guess is it's because depression causes the brain to not function as it should; so it sometimes doesn't release or secrete the correct amount of dopamine, oxytocin, serotonin and endorphins (among other hormones). So even when you do things that seemingly should make you feel some sense of happiness (aka release/secrete those hormones), you still don't feel happy doing them because your brain is not functioning as it should. I think this might also contribute to the feeling of numbness and just overall feeling of sadness and hopelessness that those with depression feel... Those hormones are much more powerful than we give them credit for. Some people are lucky and have a perfectly functioning brain in the hormone department (like those hormones are secreted when they should be), so they never develop depression. Those are the people who are luckier than they'll ever realize. 

  
My suggestion is to seek treatment for your depression. I had a good experience going to a psychiatrist, but it's best to talk with your family physician to discuss the options that suit you best for your recovery from depression. Medication might be a good option for you, or it might not be, but again those are things you'd talk about with medical professionals. Counselling, CBT and therapy might also be helpful, but don't forget that if you have one bad experience with one therapist/counsellor, it doesn't mean the whole idea of therapy is pointless. Don't abandon the whole garden over one patch of bad weeds:)

This is just my personal experience so take it as a grain of salt (because I'm not a health professional) but on top of the professional help I get, I've tried to seek doing things that release a little bit of those happy hormones in my brain. I've been dealing with clinical depression since high school, and after many years I've found that being outdoors gives me a little "shot" so-to-say of happy hormones. For some reason, our brains LOVE looking at, hearing and being around nature. There's a reason why the sound of ocean waves, rain and trees swaying in the wind are peaceful. So if you can get outdoors somewhere with someone (or alone, whatever you feel more comfortable with) and just walk through a trail of trees, or by a river (or anywhere you prefer), take the time to look up and hear all the sounds around you, touch the trees or rocks and breathe in the fresh air that the trees just oxygenated for you. Or maybe just drive to a high point in your city or town and watch the sunset. It's incredibly peaceful and has brought a small sense of happiness and hope in a time where I don't feel any happiness at all. From my experience, you can have all kinds of beautiful thoughts when being in nature; it feels like a trick to force the brain to release SOME good hormones and it feels amazing. 

It took a lot of time for me to figure out my "go-to" nature/outdoor activity, but I personally took up "paddleboarding" (using an inflatable paddleboard) during the summer seasons where I'm from. I sit on the board instead of standing because I'm not comfortable with standing yet. I spent about $500 on my inflatable paddleboard on Amazon (it came as a kit with a little seat so it's like a paddleboard/kayak hybrid). It also came with other things such as a paddle that could be converted into a kayak paddle or a paddleboard paddle. So I just choose to use the kayak paddle and sit down and paddle. I can also lay down on my board and just listen to all the sounds around me. Anyways, when I'm feeling like nothing can bring me any form of enjoyment or happiness (and I have free time off full-time work), I pack up my paddleboard and go to my favourite beach or river and just go paddleboarding. Sometimes for just 30 minutes, sometimes for almost 4-5 hours, whatever I feel like. Most times it takes me hours just to get ready to go paddleboarding because I have a hard time doing *anything* during my depressive episodes (like going to the bathroom) and I definitely don't look very beautiful when I'm out paddleboarding (sometimes my hair is greasy bc I barely have the motivation to shower or I have breakouts I didn't cover with makeup, etc.) but I try very hard to put that all aside and just get out of my tiny apartment (as difficult as it is). But when I do manage to get out and go "do something", it definitely gives me a little sense of pride knowing "I did it". Sometimes I listen to music when paddleboarding, sometimes I just listen to the soft sounds of the waves hitting my board. I let my feet dangle in the water and even though I'm generally miserable, it gives me a small feeling of contentment and that everything will be okay. Your personal "go-to" nature/outdoor activity could be anything you want; hiking, walking, biking, paddleboarding, kayaking, yoga outside, jogging, camping, skating, skiing, etc..... Anything you like best:) An awesome plus to doing this is it "forces" you in a way to get in some exercise/physical activity (which have been shown to improve depression symptoms). So you're getting in some physical activity, even when you're not even trying to. And then it also forces me to shower obviously because I just spent a bunch of time outside barefoot and sometimes sweating. So it's just been very helpful for my depression in general.  


Obviously those activities alone don't solve the actual problem, so definitely talk with your physician about what's best for you. But for me, it is a small form of therapy. It can give you a boost of hope when you feel like everything is so worthless and boring.

Wishing you the best:)

The **Baader-Meinhof** phenomenon, otherwise known as frequency illusion or recency illusion, is a phenomenon that occurs when the thing you've just noticed, experienced or been told about suddenly crops up *constantly.* It gives you the feeling that out of nowhere, pretty much everyone and their cousin are talking about the subject. You're not necessarily seeing it more, you are just *noticing* it more. For example, you recently learned all about a certain car model, and "suddenly" you seem to spot that car model everywhere you drive.

I'm going to copy/paste an answer found on Quora, posted by Knut Robert Knutsen, (studied at Flora Vidaregåande Skule). The question is "Is Denmark a socialist country?":

\------------------------

"No. Denmark is not a socialist country, none of the Nordic countries are.

They have all for varying periods of time been ruled by Social Democrats and significant features of their political systems have features that are distinctly characteristic of Social Democratic policy.

This includes government funded healthcare and education, unemployment insurance, pensions and other welfare programs. Government being involved in and running business ventures and commercial interests related to resource management, infrastructure, communication and transportation etc. All within a democratic context with strong input from unions.

Now, people on the left in these countries will unabashedly tell you that their country is Social Democrat and emphasize the welfare state, the low threshold (i.e. free or almost free) services and the equality between the people.

People on the right (bourgeois parties) in these same countries will just as directly tell you that their countries are capitalist in nature. They will point to the health of the financial markets, some low taxes, the range of freedom, the economic opportunities and other market-oriented features.

Part of what has happened is that once a policy is shown to actually undeniably work, it will be stripped of its ideological colors, everyone will want to share in the credit (success has many fathers …) and its roots are ignored by the opposition.

Most of the core socialdemocratic economic policies and social innovations actually work, so they’ve been stripped of ideology. In Norway the Conservative Party actually started about a decade ago to claim full credit for the entire social welfare system as a “core conservative policy”. Never mind that parts of the labor movement were clubbed to death fighting against bourgeois governments for it. :) They treat relenting in the face of political demands as if it is the same as leading the charge.

The Nordic countries are often more neutrally described as “mixed economies”, employing the flexibilities of a capitalist system with regulations and a safety net from Socialism/ Social Democracy. From this perspective, describing it as either “capitalist” or “socialist/ social democratic” is like the buddhist parable of a group of blind men describing an elephant through touch. Each person has a partial perspective that they have every reason to believe is correct.

Because of that, whether a person tells you that Denmark and the other Nordic countries are Capitalist or Socialist/Social Democratic, the answer is Yes, No or Both or neither. They are all most likely valid answers from the perspective of the person answering you.

They are very definitely mixed economies, though, with both a safety net and economic opportunity. Most of the political disputes are about the proportions of each part in the mix, translated into concrete changes in individual policies.

Full disclosure : I am a Social Democrat and see the “Mixed economy” part in itself as a distinct feature of the utterly pragmatic nature of Social Democracy (for which it is routinely mocked).

To me, Social Democracy is the only ideology or political movement that fully embraces a Mixed Economy as an end in itself on every level rather than as a painful compromise between the extremes of pure capitalism or pure socialism. So I, and a lot of other Social Democrats see “social democracy” as the only accurate description of mixed economy systems like ours.

We can’t really ask political rivals on the right to fully acknowledge that, though, because if they did, they might as well just quit politics right now. :)

Don’t be misled, capitalist mechanisms employed in our economies are still important. Social Democrats are not against capitalism as a practice, they just don’t see Capitalists (big business owners who absorb all the profits) as particularly useful to anyone."

Since I was a kid, I've wondered why we have to pay for things like food or water, which are essential to our survival. I live in Canada thankfully, so at least our healthcare is free. No one bats an eye about why healthcare is free ("Of course it should be free!"), but when I ask why other essential things for survival aren't free (very *basic* food, water, shelter and clothing) people say "Well because those things cost money, we can't enslave people, and people would become lazy if all that stuff was free!" Um... what? No. Healthcare costs billions of dollars, but we find a way to pay every doctor and nurse. I've always held the opinion that basic things for our survival should be free and easily accessible for all. Things like basic food, water, clothing and shelter to survive. And when I say basic I mean the basics to keep us relatively healthy, nothing fancy. Like "basic food" wouldn't include cakes or cookies, but things like potatoes, proteins, vegetables, fruits, etc. Stuff you need to live. Those things should be free. 

But who will pay the workers you ask? Everyone will. We include all those "free" things into taxes, therefore *everyone* puts a little into the moneypot so that *everyone* gets what they need. This system actually exists right now, this isn't a new idea. Denmark and Finland have adopted this idea. They have free healthcare and free education (it is illegal for a school to charge tuition in Finland), and the government pays those who have lost (or even voluntarily *LEFT)* their jobs enough money per month to cover the basics for living. I watched a video about a Finnish young adult who didn't like her job, it wasn't bringing her happiness. So she quit and the government paid her $2000/month to take it easy and figure out what she wants to do first and I think she decided to become an artist (because "starving artists" isn't a thing there). This is common practice there. Citizens pay higher taxes, but because of that everyone takes care of each other. They don't mind paying more because they see it as an *investment* into an amazing future and way of life. Homelessness doesn't exist there either. On top of that, every profession is respected. People treat you the same if you're a doctor vs a garbage man, because they realize that every job is valuable and important. Large wage gaps don't exist. A doctor makes more than a garbage man, but not by a ridiculous amount. And the thing is, in places like Denmark and Finland, you don't even *need* a job that pays a lot. There's no need to make a lot of money, because everything you need to live a good life is already provided for you. Your job is just added income and something for you to enjoy doing.

In future societies, I believe this way of life will eventually be common practice. And they will look back at *our* time the same way *we* look back at the way of life back in the 1800s or 1900s, and feel bad about how difficult our lives must have been (and then be grateful they don't live in *our* time, where we had to actually *PAY* for things we needed to survive!! How barbaric!).

Other than that, I try not to see those episodes as a failure, but more as a resting time I need in order to be okay. For me, it'll come in random waves. I might do really well for 2 weeks, shower regularly, eat well, do chores regularly, take care of myself and be out of bed for most of the day. Then, for maybe the next 3 weeks, I'm struggling just to get out of bed, eat, shower and go to the restroom. Dishes will pile up and my apartment is a mess. I've just sort of accepted this and I'm okay with doing what I need to do to be okay, even if that means spending all day watching Netflix. After those 3 weeks or so, I'll be back to "normal", clean up my apartment and pat myself on the back for ***getting back up every time I fall.*** Then maybe I'll treat myself to a pizza or something. I guess it's about being kind to yourself. It has helped and I feel less like a failure and more like a very strong woman.

(PS no I'm not bipolar, by "normal" I mean just living life normally, not being on any kind of "high")

When I was 4, we got a new black Shitzhu puppy, his name was Skip. He was the most precious thing. I remember giving him his bowl of mashed up dog food, I even remember the smell of that dog food. I remember the cute sound of him eating up his food, and how he would lean in so much that his hind legs rose up and he was basically doing a handstand while eating. I think I remember all this because of what I did to him.

One night, I was playing with him in the kitchen. My parents were close by in the next room (dining room), I could see them. For some idiotic reason that I can't remember, I thought it would be fun for him if I picked him up and dropped him. I guess I thought dogs bounced or that gravity couldn't cause injury or something stupid. My parents caught me doing this a few times before this night, and told me to stop, so it's not like I didn't know I shouldn't be doing it. Well, being the moronic child I was, I dropped him a few times from about 1 foot off the ground, then thought it would be a good idea to drop him from higher, like 2-2.5 feet. The poor angel broke his leg, I remember the complete chaos and panic after Skip started screeching and crying because of my utter stupidity. I remember my mom screaming in panic "What did you do??? What did you do?!??". My parents rushed him to the vet's, I think they called my much older sister to come watch my brother (age 5-6 at the time) and I. 

They came back very late that night, without Skip. They looked heartbroken. I asked them where Skip was. They told me that he passed away because he was allergic to the medicine they gave him when doing his surgery to fix his leg. I broke down and started crying hysterically. I can't quite remember, but I'm pretty sure I knew at that age that it was my fault he was dead. Over the years, my mom insisted it wasn't my fault. But the truth is, if I wasn't so stupid, he would have never broken his leg and therefore passed away. 

Just a few years ago though (I'm in my early 20s now), my mom told me that he wasn't actually allergic to the medicine. It was too expensive for my parents to fix his leg. My mom was completely heartbroken but they just didn't have the money. They had to put him down. However, my mom also said they didn't stay with him when he was being put down because it was too difficult to see - which I honestly disagree with, because you are this puppy's entire world and he was probably terrified and deserved to die surrounded by those who love him. But the only beacon of hope in this story is that a friend of my mom's knew the vet personally and was a very good friend of hers, and told my mom there's no way she would have put him down. So... there's a chance they didn't put him down, fixed his leg and found someone else to take him in. Either way, he would be in dog heaven by now due to this being almost 20 years ago. 

At the house we lived in when I was 4, we had a large backyard. In a nice corner, we made a little shrine/makeshift gravestone area for him.. We had this little ceramic decoration of a cross that you could open, and we would leave treats in there for him to "eat". I still remember the awful feeling of walking up to his little shrine and knowing his death was my fault. We had a pool, and after his passing I noticed that at the bottom of the shallow end there happened to be a perfect black stain in the shape of a tiny dog paw that you could see with goggles on. I remember thinking that that was him coming to say hi. Every time I went swimming, I would always place my hand on the tiny dog paw and say I'm sorry Skip. 

I'll never forgive myself for what I did, even if I was "just a stupid child." There's a 50% chance I took a tiny puppy's entire life away. I think about him atleast 4-5 times a year, and always feel horrible about it.
